extraction.name: ChartQA: A Benchmark for Question Answering about Charts with Visual and Logical Reasoning
extraction.description: Charts are very popular for analyzing data. When exploring charts, people often ask a variety of complex reasoning questions that involve several logical and arithmetic operations. They also commonly refer to visual features of a chart in their questions. However, most existing datasets do not focus on such complex reasoning questions as their questions are template-based and answers come from a fixed-vocabulary. In this work, we present a large-scale benchmark covering 9.6K human-written questions as well as 23.1K questions generated from human-written chart summaries. To address the unique challenges in our benchmark involving visual and logical reasoning over charts, we present two transformer-based models that combine visual features and the data table of the chart in a unified way to answer questions. While our models achieve the state-of-the-art results on the previous datasets as well as on our benchmark, the evaluation also reveals several challenges in answering complex reasoning questions.
extraction.creator: Ahmed Masry, Do Xuan Long, Jia Qing Tan, Shafiq Joty, Enamul Hoque
extraction.citeAs: Masry, A., Long, D. X., Tan, J. Q., Joty, S., & Hoque, E. (2022). ChartQA: A Benchmark for Question Answering about Charts with Visual and Logical Reasoning. arXiv preprint arXiv:2203.10244.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The benchmark covers 9,608 human-written questions and 23,111 questions generated from human-written chart summaries. It consists of 20,882 charts curated from four online sources: Statista, The Pew Research, Our World In Data (OWID), and Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). For Pew, only chart images were crawled. For Statista, OWID, and OECD, underlying data tables, metadata (title, chart type), SVG files, and associated text descriptions were extracted. Bounding box information of chart elements was extracted from SVG files for training data extraction models.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: For the Pew dataset, we only crawled chart images since the underlying data tables are not available.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Charts were crawled from four different online sources: Statista (statista.com), The Pew research (pewresearch.org), Our World In Data (ourworldindata.org), and Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (oecd.org).
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The pipeline first extracts the underlying data table from the chart image by adapting the ChartOCR model (Luo et al., 2021) as well as the visual features from the chart image using neural models. This involves locating main elements and data-encoding marks using key-point detection networks, recognizing texts using CRAFT model, estimating chart scale, and aggregating extracted data values using color and proximity heuristics to output fully-structured data tables with textual labels. For machine-generated questions, a heuristic was used to filter out invalid questions if the answer could not be found in the chart data table. The test set of the machine-generated dataset was manually cleaned by removing invalid questions.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human-authored QA pairs were collected using Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT). Crowdworkers were asked to provide two compositional questions (containing at least two mathematical/logical operations) and visual questions (referring to visual attributes like color, height, length) for each chart image, along with their answers. The same questions were then answered by another annotator. If both workers’ answers exactly matched, the answer was considered correct. Otherwise, answers were manually checked to select the final correct answer. Additionally, 23,111 questions were automatically generated from human-written chart summaries using a fine-tuned T5 model. This involved training two T5 models: one for answer extraction from textual summaries and another for answer-aware question generation.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The agreement between crowdworkers based on exact matches was 61.04%. After manually checking 500 random samples and considering typos or lexical variations, the agreement was found to be 78.55%. For machine-generated questions, a manual analysis of 1,250 QA pairs found 86.64% to be complete, answerable, and correct. The test set of the machine-generated dataset was manually cleaned.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 2 QA pairs per chart, with each answer verified by a second annotator.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Workers with an acceptance rate of 95% and total accomplished HITs of 5000 were selected. A pre-test was given to further filter workers. Annotators were compensated $0.6 USD per task, considering the minimum wage in the United States ($7.25 USD per hour) and an estimated task time of 3-5 minutes.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: T5 model (Raffel et al., 2020), ChartOCR model (Luo et al., 2021), CRAFT (Baek et al., 2019)
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Our models can be abused to mislead the public about the charts content and implications. While our models provide state-of-the-art results on most of the existing datasets, we can not guarantee that their output will be correct all the time.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The performance of our models decreases when the gold data table was not given. This highlights the increasing challenge of automatic data extraction from real-world charts with diversity in styles. VisionTaPas does not support nested arithmetic operations which are prevalent in ChartQA. Performance is lower for visual questions which refers to chart elements. Current approaches for automatic data extraction are modular and combine deep learning and rule-based methods which are error-prone. A major limitation of evaluation metrics for the chart data extraction is that they do not take the extracted textual tokens into consideration (which are much more noisy in real-world figures).
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, Validation, Fine Tuning. The dataset is intended for developing Chart Question Answering (ChartQA) systems that take a chart and a natural language question as input and predict the answer.
